en: The Fiftieth Collection of Birth Stories (Jātaka Paṇṇāsanipāta),
Chapter on Niḷinikā.
The Niḷinikā Jātaka:
“The countryside is burning up,
and even the kingdom is perishing.”
“Come, Niḷinikā, go;
bring that brahmin to me.
“I am not one who can endure suffering, O King.”
"I am not skilled in travel;
how shall I go to the forest frequented by elephants?"
“Having gone to a prosperous country by means of elephant, chariot,
and wooden carriage,”
"Go thus, Niḷinikā! Let the kṣatriyas go taking with them elephants,
horses, chariots, and infantry."
“By your very complexion and form,
you will bring him under your power.
“He who has the plantain tree as his banner and sign,”
Surrounded by his followers,
this delightful hermitage of Isisinga is visible.
This is reckoned as the sign of fire;
this smoke is seen.
I think it does not diminish the fire.
“Isisiṅga is of great psychic power.
And having seen her approaching,
adorned with earrings of loosened pearls, she said:
Terrified, he entered the hermitage, which was thatched with leaves;
and she was at the entrance of the hermitage.
She plays with a ball,
displaying her limbs,
both those that are secret and those that are manifest.
And seeing him playing thus,
the matted-hair ascetic who had gone to his leaf-hut emerged from the hermitage.
He spoke these words:
"O friend, what indeed is the name of that tree from which this fruit has come?"
"Even when cast far away, it returns;
it does not depart leaving that behind.
"O Brahmā, for me, this is like a horse's..."
Near Gandhamādana there are many such trees,
of which this fruit is but one part.
"Even when cast far away, it returns;
it does not depart leaving me behind.
"Let your honor come to this hermitage; let him enter."
I offer you both food and drink; please accept them.
Here is a seat; may your honor sit here.
May your honor partake of these roots and fruits from this place.
What is this on the space between your thighs that appears so well-smeared, like a black mark?
Being asked, tell me the meaning of this.
“How did your head come to enter [the mouth]?
“While I was wandering in the forest seeking roots and fruits,
I encountered a hyena of most terrifying form.”
Thus, having fallen upon me,
he suddenly seized me and tore out my head.
Now this wound itches and is eaten away.
At all times I find no comfort;
pray, sir, remove this itch for me.
Grant what you have been asked, for the sake of the brahmin.
“Your wound is deep and bloody,
its discharge is foul-smelling and great;
I shall prepare for you a certain application of astringents.”
"So that you, sir, may become supremely happy.
"Neither mantras nor medicinal decoctions,
nor herbs, O practitioner of the holy life, take effect [on one who has reached the end]."
“With that which is soft, remove your itch,
so that I may become supremely happy. “By which path,
sir, does one reach your hermitage from here?”
"Are you finding delight in the forest?
Is there plenty of roots and fruits for you?
And do the wild beasts not harm you?"
“Straight to the north of here,
from the Himalayas, flows the auspicious river Khemā;
on its bank is my delightful hermitage.”
"Oh, sir, behold my hermitage!
Mangoes, sal trees, tilakas, and rose-apples,
along with uddālakas and trumpet-flowers, are all in full bloom."
Chanted all around by Kinnaras:
"Oh, may you behold my hermitage!
Here, for me, are palm trees, roots, and fruits."
Endowed with beauty and fragrance,
and possessing a form enriched by its various grounds—
oh, may you behold my hermitage!
There is an abundance of fruits and roots here,
endowed with color, fragrance,
and flavor; and hunters come to that place.
“May they not take my roots and fruits from there.
“My father has gone out in search of roots and fruits;
he will return now at the time of evening.”
"Let us both go together to that hermitage,
until our father returns with roots and fruits.
"There are many other seers of noble character," [he replied].
The Rajis dwell along the path;
ask them about my hermitage,
and they will lead you to my presence.
“Your firewood has not been split,
nor has water been brought for you;
even the fire has not been tended by you.”
Why do you meditate as if you were dull-witted?
The wood is split, the fire has been offered,
and your fellow celibates have also finished their heat-inducing practice.
I have both a seat and water;
you, O Brahmin, delight in being before me.
You are one who has not split wood nor brought water.
"Your fire has not been kindled, nor have you eaten your meal;
you do not speak to me today.
What mental suffering, then, must you have lost?"
“Here has come a matted-hair ascetic, a practitioner of the holy life,
beautiful to behold, well-proportioned, and disciplined;
neither too tall nor too short.”
With black coverings that are very dark,
his beard is not grown and his complexion is not aged;
moreover, there is a supporting mark upon his throat.
Two well-formed breasts grew upon his chest,
radiant and resembling golden *tinduka* fruits;
and his face was exceedingly beautiful to behold.
And they hang from his ears with curled tips;
these shine as the young man wanders,
as does the thread that binds his matted locks.
And four other restraints he had—
blue, yellow, red, and white—
which ground down that young man as he wandered about.
Like Tiriṭisaṅghāriva during the rainy season,
he does not wear a girdle made of muñja grass,
nor does he spread one out, nor even for the sake of his renunciation.
They clung to the space between her thighs,
shimmering like lightning in the sky;
they were without stalks and without stems.
Attached to the waist below the navel,
they play constantly without being struck.
O Father, what kind of tree fruits are those?
And his matted locks were most beautiful to behold,
numbering more than a hundred, with curled tips and fragrant;
his head was well-proportioned, appearing as if divided into two parts.
"Oh, would that my matted locks were just like his!
And when he shakes those matted locks,
they are endowed with such beauty and fragrance!"
Just like a blue lotus shaken by the wind,
so too does this person waste away;
his state is as deplorable as a mire.
Such as this is my body, it moves when stirred by the breeze,
like a forest in full bloom at the height of summer.
He strikes down a tree fruit from the earth—
beautiful in form, lovely, and pleasing to behold—
and though it is cast away, it returns again to his hand.
"Ha! Father, what kind of tree-fruit is this?
Its teeth are most beautiful to behold—pure, even, and shaped like excellent conch shells."
They find delight in the mind as it is being opened;
surely he did not eat together with them.
It is not harsh, not stuck, but soft at every moment.
His speech is upright, neither arrogant nor fickle;
it is lovely, with a voice as sweet as the karavīka bird’s,
reaching the heart and truly delighting my mind.
Your voice is faltering and your speech is not very clear;
surely you have not applied yourself sufficiently to your recitation.
I wish, sir, to see you once again.
For indeed, young man, there was a friend before me.
This wound was well-knit on all sides, like a scar that has healed;
it is broad, well-formed, and covered with tough bark.
Then that young man, having raised me up,
pressed against my thighs with his groin.
They burned, they shone, and they gleamed.
His arms were as radiant as lightning in the sky;
his soft arms, with hair like collyrium,
shone with their variegated, rounded fingers.
Not rough-skinned nor long-haired,
his nails were long with red tips;
embracing with soft arms—
Beautiful in form, he waited upon him, delighting him.
His hands were like cotton-wool, radiant, with the lovely, round,
golden complexion of a golden bracelet.
"O Father, those hands were soft;
having touched me with them, they now burn me as they have gone from here.
Surely he did not take away the salve for wounds."
Surely he did not break the wood himself;
surely he does not strike the trees with an axe,
for there are no spikes upon his hands.
He indeed made a cut upon his wound and said to me,
"Make me happy. I did so for him,
and by that act, there was happiness for me.
Then Brahmā said to him, "I am happy.
But this bed of māluva leaves of yours has been scattered about by me and by him.
Exhausted in body, having enjoyed ourselves in the water,
we repeatedly go to our leaf-huts.
Today, dear father, no verses occur to my mind.
Neither the fire-sacrifice nor the ritual system of sacrifice,
nor even those roots and fruits shall I eat,
so long as I do not see that practitioner of the holy life.
Surely you too understand, dear father,
in which direction the practitioner of the holy life dwells;
lead me quickly, dear father, to that direction.
May I not die in this grove of the Immortals.
For I have heard that this forest is filled with variegated blossoms,
resounded by birds, and frequented by flocks of winged creatures.
"Lead me quickly to that forest, dear father,
before I give up my life in this hermitage.
"In this Jotirasa forest," he said, "I shall lead you."
In this eternal abode of the seers, frequented by hosts of gandhabbas and celestial nymphs,
do not fall into such discontent.
Friends come into being and then they cease to be;
one shows affection toward kinsmen and friends.
But where is this wretch established? To whom does he belong?
He who does not even know from where he has come—
friendships are indeed formed again and again through living together.
One who is a friend becomes estranged through lack of association;
one ages through non-association.
But if you should see one who leads the holy life...
But if you engage in debate with one who leads the holy life,
you will quickly lose this quality of asceticism,
just as a field rich in grain is destroyed by a great flood.
If you should again see a practitioner of the holy life,
and if you should again converse with that practitioner of the holy life—
just as one might pour abundant water into a vessel already full.
"You will quickly cast off this feverish state.
For these beings, my dear, wander in the world of men in various forms."
A wise man should not cultivate those [habits];
by falling under their influence, a practitioner of the holy life perishes.
Thus ends the first Niliṇikā Jātaka.
